subject: Physics
topic: Newton's laws of motion — mixed tiers
description: Inertia, F=ma, action-reaction, real-world examples, common misconceptions

questions.stem: Newton's First Law of Motion is also known as the:
questions.explanation: First Law (Inertia, 1687) — 'Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to change that state.' Galileo first articulated the idea; Newton formalised. Real-world: passengers jerk forward when a bus brakes (their bodies tend to keep moving). Three types of inertia — inertia of rest, inertia of motion, inertia of direction. SI unit of inertia: mass (kg).

questions.stem: Newton's Second Law gives the relation:

options.option_text: F = m·a (rate of change of momentum)

questions.explanation: Second Law: F = ma, derived from F = dp/dt where p = mv (momentum). For constant mass m, F = m × (dv/dt) = ma. SI unit of force = kg·m/s² = newton (N). 1 newton accelerates 1 kg by 1 m/s². Earth's gravity g ≈ 9.81 m/s², so a 1 kg object weighs ~9.81 N. F = ½mv² is kinetic energy, not force. p = mv is momentum (kg·m/s).

questions.stem: A force of 200 N acts on a body of mass 50 kg. The acceleration produced is:
questions.explanation: Apply Newton's Second Law: a = F/m = 200/50 = 4 m/s². Friction is assumed negligible. Verify by reverse calculation: F = m·a = 50 × 4 = 200 N ✓. SI unit check: N / kg = (kg·m/s²) / kg = m/s² ✓.

questions.stem: The recoil of a gun when fired is best explained by:

options.option_text: Newton's Third Law (and conservation of momentum)

questions.explanation: Third Law — 'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.' Bullet pushed forward; gun pushed backward (recoil). Conservation of momentum: total momentum before = 0. After firing: m_bullet × v_bullet + m_gun × (−v_gun) = 0 → v_gun = (m_bullet / m_gun) × v_bullet. Heavier gun → smaller recoil velocity. Same principle: rocket propulsion (gases ejected back, rocket pushed forward).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Newton's laws of motion — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A 100-g bullet is fired from a 5-kg gun with a muzzle velocity of 400 m/s. The recoil velocity of the gun is:
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum (initial total = 0): m_bullet × v_bullet = m_gun × v_recoil. 0.1 × 400 = 5 × v_recoil. So v_recoil = 40 / 5 = 8 m/s. Direction is opposite to bullet's motion. Notice the units carefully: 100 g = 0.1 kg, otherwise the answer would be 8000 m/s — clearly wrong.

questions.stem: When a person walks on the ground, the FORCE that propels them forward is the:

options.option_text: Frictional reaction of the ground on the foot (Newton's 3rd Law)

questions.explanation: When walking, your foot pushes BACKWARD on the ground (action). The ground pushes the foot FORWARD with an equal force (reaction) — friction provides this reaction. On a frictionless surface (like ice or polished marble) you can't walk effectively. Astronauts on the moon use a different push because of low gravity — but they also rely on regolith friction. Without friction, only forward momentum carries you, which dies on the next step.

questions.stem: An astronaut floats freely inside a spacecraft orbiting Earth. The reason for this 'weightlessness' is:

options.option_text: There is no gravity at orbital altitude
The astronaut and spacecraft are both in continuous free-fall around Earth
The spacecraft is moving faster than light

questions.explanation: At ISS altitude (~400 km), Earth's gravity is still ~89% of surface value — so it's NOT 'no gravity'. The spacecraft is in continuous free-fall (orbit = perpetual fall around Earth, balanced by tangential velocity). Inside, both the astronaut AND the cabin accelerate towards Earth at the same g — the astronaut feels no contact force from any surface = 'weightless'. Same effect: a person in a free-falling lift feels weightless.
